squeeze/input: Here is a handwritten digit, twenty eight by twenty eight pixels: seven hundred and eighty four numbers. Call them x.
squeeze/encode: An encoder, an ordinary network of layers, maps x down: to two hundred and fifty six hidden units, then to just sixteen numbers. Those sixteen are the code, z.
squeeze/decode: A decoder, a second network, mirrors it: from sixteen back up to two hundred and fifty six, then to seven hundred and eighty four. Its output is the reconstruction, written x hat: the hat marks x as the network rebuilt it.
squeeze/ratio: The narrow middle is the bottleneck. Each number of the code has to stand for seven hundred and eighty four over sixteen: forty nine numbers of the input.
loss/target: How is it trained? There are no labels here. The target is the input itself: the output should come back equal to x.
loss/diff: So compare them entry by entry. Say x is one, zero and two, and x hat is a half, zero and three. The differences are a half, zero, and minus one.
loss/square: Square them and add: a quarter, plus zero, plus one, which is one point two five. That squared error is the loss, L equals the norm of x minus x hat, squared. The double bars, read “norm”, give a vector's size as an arrow, the square root of its squared entries added up, so its square is just this sum of squares.
loss/train: A miss in either direction counts. Gradient steps on this loss train the encoder and the decoder together, and any pile of unlabeled images will do.
why/shapes: Each weight matrix is outputs by inputs. The encoder has two fifty six by seven eighty four, then sixteen by two fifty six. The decoder mirrors it: two fifty six by sixteen, then seven eighty four by two fifty six.
why/wide: Why squeeze at all? Make the middle as wide as the input, and the network can simply copy x through. The loss drops to zero, and the code has learned nothing about digits.
why/narrow: With sixteen numbers, copying is impossible. To rebuild the image anyway, the code has to keep what matters most: the shape of the stroke, its slant, its thickness.
